sections.title: Name and identification
sections.text: Hydnum repandum, the wood hedgehog, is a cap-and-stem fungus with a distinctive fertile underside of soft downward-pointing teeth, not gills or pores. The irregular cap is usually about 4–15 cm across, creamy white to buff or pale ochre, with a finely velvety or matte surface, a long inrolled then wavy margin and occasional shallow depressions. The fragile cream teeth are about 2–6 mm long and descend onto the firm, solid pale stem. Flesh is white and firm to brittle; handling may cause reddish or orange staining, but that change varies. A mature spore print is white. Odour is not consistently distinctive.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: It forms ectomycorrhizal associations with woodland trees and fruits from the soil among moss and leaf litter, in broadleaf or conifer woodland. Fruitbodies may stand in small groups, arcs or rings. In Britain and Ireland the main season is August to December, though timing changes with region and weather. A mushroom merely growing near a log should not be assumed to be attached to it.

sections.title: Similar species and taxonomic limits
sections.text: Hydnum rufescens, also present in this atlas, is typically smaller and more orange-brown; its teeth generally stop at or only just meet the stem instead of running clearly down it. These field distinctions overlap. Molecular studies have found multiple closely related, sometimes cryptic European Hydnum lineages, so a photo may support a Hydnum identification without proving H. repandum in the strict sense. The chanterelle has blunt folds rather than individually projecting teeth; Hericium erinaceus has a compact tooth-bearing mass on wood without a separate cap and stem.

sections.title: Edibility and caution
sections.text: The German Mycological Society and Swiss VAPKO list H. repandum as edible. Young firm specimens are preferred; old ones can be bitter. Turn over every cap to see the teeth, verify its soil habitat and other features, and do not use this plate as the sole basis for eating wild mushrooms. Seek expert confirmation of uncertain material. Cook collected mushrooms thoroughly and avoid decaying specimens; obtain medical advice if illness follows ingestion.

traits: Irregular matte creamy white to buff cap, usually 4–15 cm, margin first inrolled then wavy
Soft fragile cream teeth 2–6 mm long under cap, running down the stem; no gills
Firm pale solid stem and white flesh; reddish or orange handling stain is variable
From soil among moss or leaf litter in broadleaf or conifer woodland, late summer to autumn/early winter
safetyNote: Listed as edible, especially while young and firm, but old specimens can become bitter and related Hydnum species may be difficult to separate. Check the distinct downward teeth, soil habitat and all features; do not eat a wild specimen identified only from this plate. Ask an expert when uncertain and seek medical advice after illness.
